                                                                                 4 ShadowMem

                                                                                 Next, we present ShadowMem, the first framework to leverage agen-
                                                                                 tic memory as a defensive primitive against long-horizon attacks.
                                                                                 §4.1 motivates its design; §4.2 details each component; and §4.3
                                                                                 describes the optimization of ShadowMem for detection accuracy,
                                                                                 utility preservation, and computational efficiency.

                                                               𝑘                        • Attack success rate (ASR) measures the fraction of attack in-
                                                                                          stances in which the adversary’s malicious objective is achieved,
                                     𝑘 =𝑡                                                 quantifying the defense’s effectiveness.

where 𝛾 ∈ [0, 1) is the temporal discount factor, 𝑇 is the trajectory

horizon, and 1𝑝 is an indicator function, which returns 1 if the

predicate 𝑝 is true and 0 otherwise. Intuitively, 𝑚𝑡 receives maximal

credit from its own assessment 𝑑𝑡 and progressively attenuated

credit from more distant turns, reflecting 𝑚𝑡 ’s causal influence

along the recurrence chain.

   Format penalty. To encourage well-structured outputs con-
forming to the expected tool-call format, we apply a format penalty

(e.g., 0.1) to outputs that fail to parse correctly. When a format

violation is detected, a safe fallback is substituted: reject with a
generic rationale for the judge, or the previous memory 𝑚𝑡 −1 for
the memory manager.

   Length penalty. To encourage compact memory representa-
tions, we introduce a length penalty on the memory size:

security; Repeated-Prompt incurs the highest overhead yet pro-
vides limited defense against PI2. We therefore focus the overhead
comparison on ShadowMem, MELON, and IPIGuard, which offer
comparable security guarantees.

   Without attacks, all three incur similar overhead. Under attacks,
ShadowMem incurs lower overhead than the baselines (e.g., 2.9K vs.
3.2K and 6.8K on GPT-4o-mini). More critically, ShadowMem routes
all defense computation through a local model (e.g., Qwen3-4B),
whereas MELON and IPIGuard query the agent’s own API. Even at
comparable token counts, ShadowMem thus costs substantially less,
especially when the agent uses expensive frontier models.

6.3 Ablation Study

We conduct an ablation study to examine the external factors and
design choices that influence ShadowMem’s performance. By default,
we use GPT-4o-mini as the agent’s backbone LLM.

F.3.5 Runtime Overhead. Beyond token cost, we measure wall-
clock time on 10 long-horizon Evaluation II tasks (10.1 turns on
average) with GPT-4o-mini as the agent backbone. End-to-end task
time averages 821.1 s without defense, 207.0 s under ShadowMem,
165.3 s under MELON, and 235.8 s under IPIGuard; defended runs
are shorter because each terminates the episode once an attack is
detected, whereas the undefended agent keeps executing the full
trajectory. Isolating the defense itself, the added latency per task
is 6.13 s for ShadowMem, 4.05 s for MELON, and 6.77 s for IPIGuard,
which is small relative to the agent’s own execution time.

F.3.6 Statistical Rigor. The results reported in the main text come
from a single run per configuration. To quantify run-to-run vari-
ation, we repeat ShadowMem over 15 random seeds, varying the
decoding randomness of the agent, the attacker, and ShadowMem’s
own components while keeping the train/evaluation split, the check-
points, and all hyperparameters fixed, thus isolating inference-time
variance rather than training-seed variance. Evaluation I follows
the setting of §5.1 with GPT-5.1, and Evaluation II that of §6.1
restricted to GPT-4o-mini, with ASR averaged over the five attacks.
As Table 12 shows, the spread is small: at most 1.4 points of ASR,
0.5 points of BU, and 0.3K tokens of TC, well below the margins
by which ShadowMem improves on the undefended agent and the
baselines in Tables 1 and 5.

Table 12. Run-to-run variation of ShadowMem’s key measures, reported
as mean ± std over 15 random seeds. ASR and BU in %, TC in K tokens
per task; ASR in Evaluation II is averaged over the five attacks.

Evaluation I   ASR (↓)     BU (↑)                       TC (↓)
Evaluation II  8.3 ± 1.4  94.4 ± 0.5                   7.0 ± 0.3
               0.7 ± 0.0  59.5 ± 0.2                   2.9 ± 0.1

F.3.7 Adaptive attacks with white-box access to ShadowMem. Here,
we grant the adversary access to ShadowMem’s internals, includ-
ing model weights. In Evaluation I, following StruQ [8], we run
GCG [101] (20 suffix tokens, 500 steps) to optimize an adversarial
suffix appended to the user query, maximizing the likelihood that
𝐽 approves the target tool calls. This attack attains only 4.2% ASR,
below even the 8.3% of the unmodified STAC attack (Table 3). The
reason is architectural: 𝐽 never reads the adversarial tokens; it is
conditioned on the shadow memory 𝑚 (Eqn (3)), so the suffix must
